name: Safwa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Voorhoeve, Jan. 1973. Safwa as a restricted tone system. Studies in African Linguistics 4(1): 1-21.
catalog_quote: Confronted with a language like Safwa, which permits only one prominent syllable per word most linguists would probably tend to use the label stress rather than tone. [p.1] ... While I have used the feature [TONE] in the Safwa rules to be presented, Safwa prominence includes impressionistically both greater intensity and higher pitch. [p.1 fn.2] ... The present paper shows that in Safwa the prominence patterns can be related to a tonal or prosodic distinction in one vowel of each word (actually the word final vowel). If Safwa is described in this way as a restricted tone system, the surface manifestation of prominence can be accounted for in a very general way. [p.5] ... In general, only one syllable per word can be prominent in a surface representation. Only one exception to this rule has been observed in the language. The immediate action tense shows two prominent syllables in the same construction [p.5] ... The non-verbal constructions show three possible positions of the prominent syllable: Penultimate (PU), Ante-Penultimate (APU), and a phonologically conditioned variation between Word-Final or Ante-Pre-Stem-initial position (WF). [p.6] ... If I am right in considering PU prominence exceptional, a two-way distinction between APU and WF prominence seems to exist in all non-verbal constructions. The choice between these two possiblities depends on the stem and should be marked in the lexicon. [p.9]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Safwa (safw1238) is not in the catalog. The three works with stress in the title reduce to two works: (a) Mkomagu 1991, 'Tone and Accent in Kisongwe' (UDSM MA dissertation; Glottolog 85868 and the EBALL duplicate 588589 'Mkokagu') - Kisongwe is the Songwe dialect of Safwa (Glottolog song1301). The UDSM repository item is now deleted (404), but an Internet Archive copy of the record and its 2-page abstract PDF were recovered and. the abstract describes an autosegmental analysis of the 'tonal system' (verbs, nominals, adjectives, possessives, demonstratives) and gives no accent-placement statement; full text is print-only at UDSM East Africana Collection (THS EAF PL8007.T3M56) - priority high as the only other monograph-length treatment of Safwa word prosody and the only one on the Songwe dialect. (b) Philippson 1991 thesis (already held by the project from the gwen1239 search), read at pp. 424-425 and Annexe p. 504: Safwa is an 'accentual language with H* melody' with three nominal schemes - antepenult default, augment/final for a lexical class, tiny penult class - final syllable extrametrical, left-headed binary feet right-to-left; explicitly second-hand from Voorhoeve 1973. Best first-hand statement remains Voorhoeve 1973 (SAL 4(1), open access, held by the project, re-verified against page scan pp. 1, 5, 6, 9): one prominent syllable per word (pitch + intensity); nominals antepenultimate (unrestricted class), word-final/ante-pre-stem-initial for a second lexically marked class, penultimate in a closed set of 62 nouns; analysed as a restricted tone system (final-vowel [+/-tone]) with mora counting; verbs fixed per tense. Bing (automated download), Glottolog, UDSM DSpace API and the the Internet Archive were used instead.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (116-pp whole-issue scan of Studies in African Linguistics 4(1), 1973; Voorhoeve's article = pp. 3-23, journal pp. 1-21). I extracted pp. 3-24 with extracted text and rendered p.3 as an image to check the damaged footnote. All four quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators: (a) journal p.5 / p.7, sec. 2: 'In general, only one syllable per word can be prominent in a surface representation.'; (b) p.6 / p.8: 'The non-verbal constructions show three possible positions of the prominent syllable: Penultimate (PU), Ante-Penultimate (APU), and a phonologically conditioned variation between Word-Final or Ante-Pre-Stem-initial position (WF).'; (c) p.9 / p.11, sec. 3:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Culminative system: each word has (normally) exactly one prominent syllable (higher pitch + greater intensity). Where it falls is not fixed: in nouns/pronouns the stem is lexically marked for one of two patterns -- APU (prominence on the antepenultimate mora, the default; analysed as word-final vowel [-TONE] with H assigned two morae before it) or WF (word-final vowel [+TONE]: prominence goes to the augment/ante-pre-stem-initial vowel if one is present, otherwise surfaces on the final syllable); penultimate prominence is a small exceptional class (loans, underlying long finals). In verbs the position is determined by the tense (PU, APU, pre-antepenultimate = 4th mora, or fixed on a particular morpheme). Voorhoeve treats this as a 'restricted tone system' (one tonal specification per word, on the final vowel) rather than stress; Hyman 2006 likewise: obligatory one-H-mora-per-word, mora-counting, hence not stress-accent proper.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the only case of two prominences in one word is the immediate-action tense (twáganábale), analysed as two words with a reduced boundary (p.5-6).
new_statements.exceptions: PU class of ~62 nouns and some pronouns (reduplications with underlying long final vowel, loans from Swahili/Nyakyusa such as ishitála, morphemes -ene 'self', -ope 'also'); monosyllabic stems shift the patterns by one mora (ex.10, rule 11); continuative -ag-/-ang- and vocalic suffixes shift prominence one vowel rightward (ex.20-21); class 1/9 subject prefixes shift to PU in some tenses (ex.22); infinitive has fixed prominence on initial a-.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prominence in citation/elicited forms from one speaker of the Ilaambo variety; deletion of word boundary in possessive/demonstrative phrases makes the phrase a single prominence domain (amíino + giitú -> aminógiitu, p.6, rule 15). WF pattern's word-final vs augment realisation depends on predicative vs non-predicative use.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve's data are 'exclusively from Ilaambo, a village between Mbeya and the Poroto mountains' (one main speaker, C.K. Mwachusa, 1966) -- i.e. a single local variety of Safwa M25 (safw1238); Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes for Safwa. Mkomagu 1991 treats 'Kisongwe' (Songwe area variety), filed by Glottolog under Safwa. The saved PDF is the whole SAL 4(1) issue and also contains Schadeberg 1973 on Kinga (nucl1379), which must not be confused with the Safwa article (pp. 1-21).

new_statements.reading: First-hand, field-based statement. Safwa has culminative word prominence (one prominent syllable per word, realised as higher pitch plus greater intensity), but its position is not fixed: in nominals the unmarked class carries antepenultimate prominence (counted in morae; underlying long vowels count as two), a second lexically marked class puts prominence on the word-final syllable or, when an augment/initial element is present, on the ante-pre-stem-initial (augment) syllable, and a closed set of 62 nouns and some pronouns has penultimate prominence (loans, reduplications, exceptional consonants). Voorhoeve models the APU/WF split as a [+/-tone] specification on the word-final vowel, i.e. a 'restricted tone system' rather than stress; in verbs the position is fixed per tense (PU, APU, 4th mora or fixed-morpheme prominence). For catalog purposes: lexically contrastive accent placement (antepenult default vs final/augment), not fixed stress; mora-counting; penult only in an exceptional closed class. Philippson 1991 (pp. 424-425, 504) and Hyman 2006 (ex. 18a) both rest on this source.

tone_statements.translation: ...[languages which,] regardless of the number of syllables or moras, have only a fixed number of patterns (in Uwano Zendo's terminology, N-type accent) also exist. Below, in the remaining space, as an example of such a language, examples from Safwa, spoken in south-western Tanzania (from Voorhoeve 1973) ... But in present-day Safwa there are only two patterns. That is, only the tone of the first stem syllable of Proto-Bantu is effectively preserved, and underlyingly it appears on the last syllable of the word ... And in the isolation form the word-final H appears two moras before the noun stem, i.e. on the augment, and in the L case the third mora from the end of the word becomes H.

sources.locator: Ch. 4 (comparative nominal tone), sec. 2.3.2, pp. 424-425; Tableau p. 78 ('(a) : 3, (b) : 1' = safwa, groupe X); p. 81 examples; Annexe p. 504 Safwa profile
sources.note: Second-hand from Voorhoeve 1973. pp.424-425 sec.2.3.2: Safwa nominal themes fall into three schemes; penultimate accent only a handful of themes; the vast majority have accent on the antepenult (default) or on the augment if present, otherwise on the final. Annexe p.504 profile: 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*', 3 schemes, final syllable extrametrical, left-dominant binary feet built right-to-left, H associated to marked syllable. p.484: length contrast neutralised outside penult/antepenult ('langues à accent').

tone.says: Treats Safwa as a High-tone-only ('Narrow Bantu' type) system in which many tenses are marked by assigning H to the antepenultimate mora of the word; uses Safwa uha-jeéndile to argue that mora-based antepenult H targeting violates syllable integrity under a metrical (trochee) account, and groups Safwa with Sukuma, Zezuru Shona and Xhosa as cases where ALIGN/*ALIGN target the third TBU from an edge.

tone.quote: Guthrie comments that tone in Kisafwa is “fully distinctive but opaque” (1971). After comparing the first 50 nouns for which all six locations had the same lexical item, little disagreement in tone pattern was found. … Regarding the imperative tone patterns, CVCV 13 stems behave the same across the varieties (210), but stems of other syllabic structure do not. For CV:CV stems (275), Mjele has a high tone on the final mora 14, whereas the other varieties have it on the penultimate mora (or APU for Itala).

sources.quote: This study is the first attempt at analyising the tonal system of Kisongwe, using Autosegmental phonology framework. [...] Chapter one provides the problem area and the historical background to the study of Supra-Segmental, which include tone and accent. Chapter Two presents tonological processes which operate in Kisongwe Infinitival Verb forms, while chapter three discusses the same processes in Kisongwe finite Verb forms.
